Red List Authority Coordinator: Catherine Numa (email: catherine.numa@iucn.org)

documentation.range: This species is known from Brazil: Minas Gerais (Lavras, Parque Nacional da Serra da Canastra, Carrancas, São Gonçalo do Rio Preto [Parque Estadual do Rio Preto]); Mato Grosso (São Vicente da Serra in Santo Antônio de Leverger); São Paulo (São Paulo, old collections only); and and Distrito Federal (Brasilia: APA de Cafuringa). All localities are above 1,000 m asl (Blackwelder 1944, F. Vaz-de-Mello pers. comm. 2013). Based on known localities, the extent of occurrence is estimated as around 380,000 km<sup>2</sup>, although within this, the area of occupancy is much more restricted, to between 700 km<sup>2</sup> [overlaying grid of 10 km (100 km<sup>2</sup>) in size] and no more than 1,575 km<sup>2</sup> [overlaying grid of 15 km (225 km<sup>2</sup>) in size]. With currently only seven known localities, the number of locations for this species is definitely less than ten unless additional localities for this species are established via surveying and collecting.
documentation.population: There are no population data available for this species.
documentation.habitats: This species is endemic to high altitude open areas in Southeastern Brazil. Specifically, it is restricted to campo rupestre (fireprone open savanna/grassland with very shallow soil). It is most probably not tolerant of introduced artificial pastureland which surrounds habitat patches of campo rupestre habitat (F. Vaz-de-Mello pers. comm. 2013). Furthermore, since campo rupestre is part of a gradient of habitats (grading into other habitat types), campo rupestre itself is very patchy and restricted in distribution (F. Vaz-de-Mello pers. comm. 2013). Within campo rupestre, this species is more widespread than Canthon quadripunctatus (F. Vaz-de-Mello pers. comm. 2013) which has also been assessed as Vulnerable.
documentation.threats: The major threat to this species is habitat destruction for grazing. Substitution of habitat is common, due to a lack of protection for grasslands (for example when compared to protection for forest habitat), particularly for this type of very species-rich grassland. Cattle ranching poses the dominant threat to the habitat (F. Vaz-de-Mello pers. comm. 2013). Although at present, much of the habitat still remains in its natural state, only 5% of campo rupestre is currently in the federal system of protected areas (WWF 2007). Fire is also a threat, but forms part of the natural processes affecting campo rupestre habitat.
documentation.measures: There are no known species-specific conservation measures in place for this species. Better protection of grassland habitats is needed to prevent further substitution of habitat to introduced pasture for cattle grazing, and protect remaining fragments of species rich campo rupestre habitat. Further surveys and collections are vital to establish if the species occurs in additional localities in campo rupestre, as records of additional localities may reduce its extinction risk category in the future.
documentation.use_trade: This species is unlikely to be utilized.
documentation.rationale: Canthon corpulentus has been assessed as Vulnerable under criterion B2ab(iii), based on its restricted area of occurrence of around 1,575 km2, and number of locations (currently only seven localities are known, resulting in no more than ten locations). Campo rupestre is a highly species-rich, restricted grassland type of very shallow soil, which forms part of a habitat gradient and hence is only patchy in distribution. Since the species is unlikely to tolerate substituted artificial grassland which surrounds campo rupestre, it is likely that there is no or hardly any movement between campo rupestre patches, thus also causing fragmentation. With the continuing threat of substitution of native campo rupestre grassland with grazed land and a lack of protection afforded to grasslands, the extent and quality of the habitat of this species is likely to be further reduced. Similarly, additional surveying might also confirm a continuing decline in the area of occupancy for this species. As a result, further surveying and collecting at and around the known localities and in other campo rupestre patches is needed to establish if there are any more localities for this species. If new localities are found, the status of this species might be reduced to NT in future reassessments. Any future indication of pastureland association would lower extinction risk status even further. However, at present such an association is thought to be unlikely.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
A review of Canthon lamproderes by Fernando Vaz-de-Mello will soon be published which places some specimens previously identified as Canthon lamproderes within Canthon corpulentus - this has been taken into account in this assessment.


Canthon is a diverse and heterogeneous genus of dung beetles. Currently, the genus is composed of nine subgenera: Boreocanthon, Canthon s.str., Francmonrosia, Glaphyrocanthon, Goniocanthon, Nesocanthon, Peltecanthon, Pseudepilissus, and Trichocanthon. Of these, only Boreocanthon and Nesocanthon do not occur in South America. The genus is taxonomically relatively well known.
